title: Documentation and knowledge bases
monthTitle: The Helpdesk Professional: ITIL, Ticketing & Soft Skills
summary: Learn to write ticket notes and knowledge-base articles that other technicians and users can actually follow, turning each solved problem into reusable knowledge.
objectives: Explain why documentation is a core helpdesk responsibility, not an afterthought
Write clear, factual ticket notes that capture what was done and why
Structure a knowledge-base (KB) article a user or technician can follow
Distinguish internal documentation from user-facing articles
Apply knowledge-centred service principles in everyday work
Write a usable KB article from a solved ticket

quiz.q: Why is documentation considered part of the actual job, not extra work?
options: It turns solved issues into reusable knowledge and lets others continue your work
quiz.why: Good notes let any technician resume or repeat a fix without re-investigating, and KB articles deflect future tickets, so documentation directly multiplies the team's capacity.

quiz.q: What makes a good knowledge-base article?
options: Lots of jargon to sound expert
A clear title, the problem, numbered steps, and the expected result
quiz.why: Useful KB articles have a searchable title, a description of the symptom, clear numbered steps, and confirmation of the expected outcome so the reader knows it worked.

quiz.q: What is the difference between internal documentation and a user-facing article?
options: Internal docs can be technical; user-facing articles use plain language and avoid sensitive detail
User-facing articles are for managers only
quiz.why: Internal notes can include technical detail and tools; user-facing self-help articles use plain language and never expose sensitive internal information.

quiz.q: What does 'knowledge-centred service' (KCS) encourage technicians to do?
options: Capture and reuse knowledge as part of solving each issue
quiz.why: KCS treats knowledge capture as a by-product of solving tickets, so the knowledge base grows and improves continuously through normal work.

quiz.q: Write a good, searchable title for a KB article about resetting a forgotten domain password. Explain your choice.
quiz.answer: Something like 'How to reset a forgotten Windows domain password (self-service)'. It names the system, the action, and the context, so users searching 'reset password' will find it.
quiz.why: A searchable title contains the words users actually type and clearly states what the article covers.

quiz.q: Why should ticket notes be factual and free of blame or opinion?
quiz.answer: Tickets are official, shared records that others read and that may be audited, so notes must state facts and actions, not opinions or criticism of users or colleagues.
quiz.why: Professional, factual notes protect everyone, stay useful over time, and avoid creating problems if the ticket is reviewed later.

body_markdown:
## Documentation is the work, not the paperwork

Many beginners treat writing things down as the annoying bit after the real work. Reframe it: on a service desk, **documentation is how your work scales**. A fix you record once can be repeated by anyone in minutes; a fix you keep in your head dies when you go to lunch. Two kinds of writing matter most: **ticket notes** and **knowledge-base articles**.

## Writing good ticket notes

Ticket notes are the running record of what happened. They should let a colleague pick up your ticket cold. Keep them **factual, chronological, and free of blame or opinion** — tickets are official records that can be audited.

```text
10:14 - User reports shared drive S: missing after reboot.
10:18 - Confirmed drive maps fine on a colleague's PC. Scope: 1 user.
10:25 - Found mapped-drive logon script not running; Group Policy
        not applied. Forced gpupdate /force - drive reappeared.
10:30 - Verified with user, S: now present and accessible. Resolved.
```

Notice it records *facts and actions with times*, not "user was clueless." Never write anything in a ticket you would not want the user, your boss, or an auditor to read.

## What a knowledge-base article is

A **knowledge base (KB)** is a searchable library of articles describing how to solve known issues. Some are **internal** (for technicians); some are **user-facing self-help** that deflect tickets entirely. A good article has a predictable structure:

```text
Title:    How to map the shared S: drive (Windows)
Applies to: Windows 11 domain PCs
Symptom:  The S: drive is missing from File Explorer
Steps:
  1. Open File Explorer and click "This PC".
  2. Click the three-dot menu, then "Map network drive".
  3. Choose drive letter S: and enter \\fileserver\shared.
  4. Tick "Reconnect at sign-in" and click Finish.
Expected result: The S: drive appears under "This PC".
```

A **searchable title** uses the words users actually type. Numbered **steps** are unambiguous. An **expected result** lets the reader confirm it worked.

## Internal vs user-facing

Internal docs can be technical and reference tools, scripts, or admin steps. **User-facing** articles use plain language, avoid jargon, and **never expose sensitive detail** such as server names or security settings the public should not see. Always ask: *who will read this?*

## Knowledge-centred service

**Knowledge-Centred Service (KCS)** is the principle that capturing knowledge should be a natural **by-product of solving tickets**, not a separate project. When you solve something new, you write or improve an article as you go. Over time the knowledge base becomes the team's collective memory, and First Contact Resolution climbs because answers are already written down.

## Your task

Take the solved ticket from earlier in the course where Sam's S: drive disappeared (or invent a similar fix you understand). Write a complete, user-facing KB article for it: a searchable title, an 'applies to' line, the symptom, numbered steps in plain language, and an expected result. Then write one sentence on what you would change if the article were internal-only instead.

Record actions with times.

10:18 - Drive maps fine on colleague's PC. Scope: 1 user.
10:25 - Logon script not running; forced gpupdate /force.
10:30 - Verified with user, S: present. Resolved.
slides.narration: First, ticket notes. These are the running record of what happened, and they should let a colleague pick up your ticket completely cold. slides.title: What a KB article is
bullets: A searchable library of known fixes.
Some internal, some user-facing self-help.
User-facing articles deflect tickets entirely.
Predictable, repeatable structure.
slides.narration: Now the knowledge base. A knowledge base, or K B, is a searchable library of articles describing how to solve known issues. Some are internal, written for technicians. Others are user-facing self-help articles that let users fix things themselves, which deflects tickets entirely before they ever reach you. The best knowledge bases follow a predictable structure, so readers always know where to find the title, the symptom, the steps, and the result.

slides.title: Anatomy of a good article
bullets: Searchable title with words users type.
Symptom: what the reader is experiencing.
Numbered, unambiguous steps.
Expected result to confirm success.
slides.code:
Title: How to map the shared S: drive (Windows)
Symptom: S: drive missing from File Explorer
Steps: 1. Open File Explorer > This PC ...
Expected result: S: appears under This PC.
slides.narration: Let's dissect a good article. It starts with a searchable title that uses the words users actually type, like map the shared S drive, not some internal code name. Then the symptom, describing what the reader is experiencing. Then numbered steps that are completely unambiguous, one action per step. And finally an expected result, so the reader can confirm it actually worked. That structure is what separates a helpful article from a confusing wall of text.

slides.title: Internal vs user-facing
bullets: Internal docs can be technical and detailed.
User-facing uses plain language.
Never expose sensitive detail to users.
Always ask: who will read this?
slides.narration: An important distinction: internal documentation versus user-facing articles. Internal docs can be technical and reference tools, scripts, or admin steps, because technicians read them. User-facing articles use plain language, avoid jargon, and crucially never expose sensitive detail, like internal server names or security settings the public shouldn't see. Before you write a single line, ask yourself the key question: who is going to read this? The answer shapes everything about how you write it.

slides.title: Knowledge-centred service
bullets: Capture knowledge as you solve tickets.
Not a separate project at year end.
Write or improve an article as you go.
The KB becomes the team's memory.
slides.narration: There's a principle that ties this together, called Knowledge-Centred Service, or K C S. The idea is that capturing knowledge should be a natural by-product of solving tickets, not a separate project you dread doing once a year. When you solve something new, you write or improve an article as you go. Over time, the knowledge base becomes the team's collective memory, and First Contact Resolution climbs, because so many answers are already written down and waiting.

slides.title: Write as you work
bullets: Document while the details are fresh.
Don't leave notes until end of day.
Small, frequent updates beat big rewrites.
Good docs make you look professional.
slides.narration: A practical habit to build: document while the details are fresh in your mind, not at the end of a long day when you've forgotten the specifics. Small, frequent updates to your notes and to the knowledge base beat one big rewrite later. And here's a career tip: clean, helpful documentation makes you look genuinely professional to your team and your managers. It's one of the easiest ways for a beginner to stand out and be trusted with more responsibility.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Documentation makes your work scale.
Ticket notes: factual, timed, no blame.
KB articles: title, symptom, steps, result.
Capture knowledge as you solve.
Task: write a user-facing KB article.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Documentation is how your work scales beyond a single fix. Ticket notes should be factual, timed, and free of blame. Knowledge-base articles need a searchable title, the symptom, numbered steps, and an expected result. And the best technicians capture knowledge as a natural part of solving tickets.
